paragraphs: 3DGS-HPC addresses a practical obstacle in reconstructing scenes from images: moving objects and changing shadows can interfere with the scene representation. These transient elements reduce the quality of views rendered from new positions. The paper focuses on distinguishing stable scene content from temporary distractors during 3D Gaussian Splatting.

The authors identify problems with two common uses of pretrained visual features. Grouping pixels by meaning does not necessarily separate static content from transient content. Meanwhile, perceptual comparisons can become unreliable as appearances change during optimization. Their approach combines decisions over local image patches with a classification measure that adaptively mixes photometric and perceptual information. Patch-level decisions exploit local spatial consistency, while the combined measure draws on complementary visual cues.

The reported experiments show improved robustness to distractors and better novel-view synthesis. The contribution is a way to make the static-versus-transient distinction more reliable within reconstruction, using both local spatial structure and adaptive evidence combination.
icml-2026-3dgs-hpc-distractor-free-3d-ga.tldr: 3DGS-HPC combines patch-level decisions and adaptive visual cues to reduce transient distractors in 3D scene reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to share information across related learning tasks when their similarities are partly hidden. Tasks belong to unknown groups with shared target parameters, but other components can differ substantially across tasks. Those nuisance components may even be infinite-dimensional, making ordinary assumptions about aligned features or homogeneous tasks unsuitable.

The proposed estimator combines two mechanisms. Adaptive pairwise fusion penalties encourage appropriate tasks to share target estimates, with initial task-specific estimates determining how fusion is calibrated. Neyman-orthogonal losses reduce sensitivity to errors in estimating nuisance components. Together, these mechanisms aim to discover which tasks should pool information while limiting interference from their differences.

The theoretical results establish exact cluster recovery with high probability, pooled parametric convergence rates linked to cluster size, and asymptotic normality. Asymptotically, the estimator matches an oracle that already knows the groups. Simulations report improvements over strong baselines, while an application to residential energy consumption identifies meaningful regional groupings in electricity price elasticity.
icml-2026-adaptive-estimation-and-infere.tldr: An adaptive estimator discovers shared task groups while reducing the influence of errors in task-specific nuisance estimates.

paragraphs: This paper develops an online method for controlling Conditional Value-at-Risk, a measure focused on the severe end of the loss distribution. Its setting allows the data-generating process to change over time, including strategic changes. That matters when rare, damaging outcomes drive system risk and stationarity assumptions are inappropriate.

The method connects conformal tail-risk control with online learning and the Rockafellar–Uryasev variational representation of CVaR. This representation provides the basis for a procedure with adversarial regret guarantees. The framework does not impose assumptions on the underlying data-generating process, extending risk control to sequences that can drift or respond adversarially.

The guarantees concern realized empirical CVaR: it is controlled at the target level asymptotically. The control also becomes asymptotically tight, with a finite-sample conservatism gap of order one over the square root of the number of observations. Demonstrations in portfolio risk management and language-model toxicity mitigation illustrate its application to tail risks. These are long-run empirical guarantees, rather than a claim that every individual outcome is safe.
icml-2026-adversarially-robust-control-o.tldr: An online framework asymptotically controls empirical tail risk even when data change arbitrarily or adversarially.

paragraphs: AudioChat targets complex audio scenes containing multiple speakers and foreground or background sound effects. The authors call these scenes audio stories. Understanding and modifying them requires handling meaning, timing, and physical relationships together, creating challenges beyond simpler audio-processing tasks. The framework brings generation, editing, and understanding into a shared system.

A central contribution is its training-data strategy. Language-model agents that can call tools simulate exchanges between users and the system, and those dialogues become training examples. The authors also introduce Audio Transfusion Forcing, a training objective that supports both structured decomposition of high-level instructions and interactive audio understanding or generation over multiple turns.

The evaluation contribution consists of three new metrics for audio generation and editing. These measure task performance directly, rather than relying on distribution-based scores. The paper therefore combines an interaction-oriented data pipeline, a unified training objective, and task-focused evaluation. Its stated contribution is this framework and its capabilities; the abstract does not report numerical performance improvements.
icml-2026-audiochat-unified-audio-storyt.tldr: AudioChat uses simulated dialogues and a unified training objective to generate, edit, and understand complex audio stories.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the speed and quality of autoregressive image generation. Conventional autoregressive models use next-token prediction to maintain causality, but their sequential prediction process creates substantial inference latency. The authors also describe a quality gap between these approaches and non-causal alternatives, including masked prediction and diffusion.

Their proposed alternative is self-token prediction, which permits a flexible number of tokens to be predicted in each step. They build SAR, a spatially autoregressive image generator, around this prediction paradigm. The key change is therefore in the unit of progress during generation: a step can produce a variable number of tokens while supporting an autoregressive approach to visual generation.

The authors report markedly faster inference and consistently better performance than earlier autoregressive baselines. They also report performance comparable to leading non-causal models. Taken together, these findings support self-token prediction as a promising way to improve both speed and image-generation quality within the autoregressive paradigm.
icml-2026-autoregression-with-self-token.tldr: SAR uses self-token prediction to generate flexible numbers of image tokens per step, improving reported speed and quality.

paragraphs: TELLME addresses the difficulty of monitoring what language models are doing internally. Written chains of thought are often used as a window into model reasoning, but the paper argues that they do not accurately reflect the underlying process. Hidden representations offer another source of information for identifying unsuitable or sensitive behavior.

The authors shift attention from building external monitoring modules to making the language model itself easier to monitor. TELLME is designed to improve model transparency so that monitors can better identify problematic behavior. The central contribution is therefore a change to the model being observed, alongside the broader use of its internal representations for monitoring.

The reported evaluation focuses on detoxification. Improvements are consistent across multimodal test sets, different architectures, and varying model sizes. The authors also examine improved generalization through both optimal transport theory and empirical analysis. These results support enhancing monitorability within the model as a useful approach to behavior detection, with evidence spanning several tested model and evaluation settings.
icml-2026-beyond-external-monitors-enhan.tldr: TELLME makes language models easier to monitor and reports consistent improvements on detoxification evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper examines a tradeoff in reducing hallucinations in vision-language models. Contrastive decoding compares expert and amateur branches at the level of token scores, or logits. The authors find that interventions at this stage compromise output coherence, requiring restrictive penalties that are separate from the goal of suppressing hallucinations.

Attention Contrastive Decoding moves part of this contrastive process earlier into the attention mechanism. It is a training-free addition designed to work alongside existing logit-level methods. Its Adaptive Subtraction Strategy weakens attention patterns associated with hallucination while strengthening important visual information. The intended effect is a smoother intervention that preserves semantic coherence during generation.

Experiments report that combining ACD with existing methods, including VCD, produces more coherent outputs and further reduces hallucinations. The combinations also remove the need for the restrictive penalties identified by the authors. The findings suggest that where a contrastive intervention occurs inside the model matters for balancing visual accuracy with readable, coherent generation.
icml-2026-beyond-logits-coherent-halluci.tldr: Attention Contrastive Decoding complements existing decoding methods to reduce hallucinations while improving output coherence.

paragraphs: LieFlow addresses automatic discovery of the symmetries present in data. Knowing these symmetries can help explain physical systems and improve machine-learning performance and sample efficiency. The challenge is to infer the relevant transformations without already specifying the precise symmetry structure that the data obey.

The framework treats discovery as learning a distribution over a larger candidate Lie group. Instead of searching directly for symmetry generators, it works with group elements themselves. The support of the learned distribution reveals the subgroup representing the underlying symmetries. This formulation accommodates both continuous and discrete symmetries without requiring a fixed Lie algebra basis or a prescribed distribution over group elements.

The authors evaluate LieFlow on synthetic two- and three-dimensional point clouds, ModelNet10, and MI-Motion data. They report accurate recovery of continuous and discrete subgroups, with especially strong improvements over LieGAN for discrete symmetries. The findings support distribution learning in group space as a unified route to identifying different kinds of symmetry.
icml-2026-discovering-symmetry-groups-wi.tldr: LieFlow learns distributions over transformation groups to discover both continuous and discrete symmetries in data.

paragraphs: DOUBT targets a weakness in detecting hallucinations from multimodal language models: repeated answers can agree with one another while still being wrong. The authors attribute this partly to a mismatch between visual and language capabilities. When visual understanding is weaker, consistency across generated answers can exaggerate trustworthiness and cause detectors to miss errors.

The method combines a prompting procedure with a trustworthiness measure. Object-level Understanding and Bridging first asks the model to identify objects, then asks it to reason from those objects. This separates recognition from relational reasoning. A von Mises–Fisher-based metric then assesses trustworthiness, with greater reported stability than semantic-entropy metrics when only a small number of samples are available.

The approach is model-agnostic, and the authors evaluate it through multiple benchmarks and ablation studies. They report consistent improvements over leading detection baselines. The findings support separating stages of visual reasoning and improving small-sample trust estimation as complementary ways to detect hallucinations more reliably.
icml-2026-doubt-decoupled-object-level-u.tldr: DOUBT separates object recognition from relational reasoning and uses a more stable trust metric to detect multimodal hallucinations.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to evaluate agents that collaborate with people. Accuracy benchmarks often assume that agents complete tasks autonomously, which leaves out an important part of practical use: whether people are satisfied with the interaction. The authors introduce PULSE to make evaluations centered on human experience more efficient.

PULSE collects user feedback, trains a model to predict satisfaction, and combines actual satisfaction ratings with model-generated pseudo-labels. The authors deploy the framework through a software-engineering platform built around OpenHands. Across 15,000 users, they examine how three agent-design decisions affect developer satisfaction, providing an evaluation grounded in real interactions.

PULSE reduces confidence intervals by 40% compared with a standard A/B test, supporting more precise conclusions about design choices. The study also finds substantial differences between benchmark performance and results in actual use, including an anti-correlation involving the compared models. The findings show why satisfaction measurements can add information that automation-focused benchmarks do not capture.
icml-2026-how-can-we-assess-human-agent-.tldr: PULSE combines user ratings with predicted satisfaction to evaluate collaborative agents more precisely in real-world use.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning tries to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving performance on the data that remain. These goals can conflict. The paper argues that combining losses with fixed weights does not guarantee specified improvements across forget and retain data, motivating an approach based on constrained optimization.

HAMU measures the difficulty of reconciling the objectives through similarity between forget and retain data. It uses this hardness measure to guide weight updates toward a specified improvement in forgetting while minimizing damage to retained utility. The measure also identifies situations where retaining utility must worsen and simultaneous improvement is impossible, providing a reason to consider stopping.

The algorithm applies to non-convex models and supports parallel execution. Experiments with large models on image and text datasets report better performance than the tested baselines. Its contribution is both an unlearning procedure and a way to assess the tradeoff: the method explicitly accounts for when removing one influence conflicts with preserving another.
icml-2026-how-hard-can-it-be-hardness-aw.tldr: HAMU uses forget–retain similarity to guide unlearning and identify when preserving retained performance conflicts with forgetting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much a pretrained graph neural network can adapt through lightweight tuning. Graph prompt tuning is a common approach, but explaining why it works does not establish the limits of what it can express. The authors introduce Prismatic Space Theory to quantify adaptation capacity and establish an upper bound for graph prompt tuning.

Using this framework, they propose Message Tuning for Graph Foundation Models. MTG adds a small collection of learnable message prototypes at every layer of the graph neural network. These prototypes guide how messages are fused while the pretrained weights remain fixed. Adaptation therefore acts directly within the network’s message-processing layers.

The theoretical result shows that MTG’s adaptation capacity can exceed the upper bound established for graph prompt tuning. This is a capacity claim, not a guarantee about every downstream task. Experiments nevertheless provide supporting evidence: MTG consistently beats graph prompt baselines across the benchmark datasets evaluated, connecting the theoretical advantage with observed task performance.
icml-2026-message-tuning-outshines-graph.tldr: Message tuning adapts frozen graph networks with learnable message prototypes whose capacity can exceed graph prompt tuning’s theoretical bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies cooperative reinforcement learning when adding another agent produces diminishing returns. That reward structure, called submodularity, captures overlapping contributions: several surveillance drones or exploring agents may provide some of the same benefit. Treating team reward as a simple sum misses this overlap.

The authors formalize this setting and develop algorithms for both known and unknown dynamics. When dynamics are known, greedy policy optimization achieves a one-half approximation with computational complexity polynomial in the number of agents. This gives a guaranteed fraction of optimal performance while avoiding the exponential dependence associated with joint policy optimization.

When dynamics are unknown, the proposed learning algorithm uses upper confidence bounds and achieves a stated one-half-regret bound over repeated episodes. This measures learning performance against an approximation benchmark rather than promising convergence to the unrestricted optimum. The contribution is theoretical: it connects the diminishing-returns structure of team rewards to tractable optimization and guarantees on learning efficiency.
icml-2026-multi-agent-reinforcement-lear.tldr: Submodular team rewards enable cooperative reinforcement-learning algorithms with polynomial optimization and provable approximation and regret guarantees.

paragraphs: MVI-Bench examines how vision-language models respond when the image itself is misleading. The authors identify a gap in robustness evaluation: existing benchmarks emphasize hallucinations or deceptive text, leaving misleading visual inputs less thoroughly assessed. Their benchmark makes this visual challenge the central object of measurement.

The benchmark organizes misleading inputs into three levels: visual concepts, visual attributes, and visual relationships. Within this structure, the authors curate six representative categories and assemble 1,248 expertly annotated visual question-answering examples. They also introduce MVI-Sensitivity, a metric intended to support more detailed assessment of model robustness across these inputs.

Evaluating 18 leading vision-language models reveals pronounced vulnerabilities. The result indicates that strong multimodal capabilities do not, by themselves, establish robustness to misleading visual evidence in these tests. The benchmark and its taxonomy provide a structured basis for examining those weaknesses, while the accompanying analyses are intended to guide improvements in visual understanding and reliability.
icml-2026-mvi-bench-a-comprehensive-benc.tldr: MVI-Bench evaluates misleading visual inputs and finds substantial robustness weaknesses across 18 vision-language models.

paragraphs: Olmix addresses how to choose the proportions of different data domains used to train a language model. The authors identify two practical problems: mixing methods contain poorly understood design choices, and training datasets change during development. A useful mixing strategy must therefore handle both initial configuration and later revisions to the domain set.

The paper first conducts an empirical study of mixing-method design, including practical data constraints. It then introduces mixture reuse for updating an existing mix. This mechanism preserves existing relative ratios and recomputes ratios only for domains affected by an update, reducing the amount of work required when datasets are revised or expanded.

Across five domain-set updates designed to mirror language-model development, mixture reuse matches the performance of fully recomputing each mixture while using 74% less compute. It also improves downstream-task performance by 11.6% over training without mixing. These findings support treating a data mixture as something that can be efficiently maintained throughout development.
icml-2026-olmix-a-framework-for-data-mix.tldr: Olmix reuses existing data-mixture ratios to maintain performance across dataset updates with substantially less recomputation.

paragraphs: This paper tackles two obstacles in protein fold classification: insufficient large benchmarks without redundant structures and representation models that scale poorly. The authors introduce TEDBench, constructed from the Encyclopedia of Domains and clustered AlphaFold structures. Their evaluation finds that existing representation-learning methods either need very large models or struggle to achieve strong performance.

The proposed Masked Invariant Autoencoder learns protein representations by reconstructing heavily masked structures. It masks up to 90% of the input and combines an SE(3)-invariant encoder with a lightweight decoder. The encoder’s invariance means its representation is unaffected by rotations and translations, while the decoder reconstructs backbone coordinates using latent representations and mask tokens.

MiAE reportedly scales well and outperforms supervised counterparts and leading baselines on TEDBench. The authors also evaluate on curated experimental structures from CATH v4.4 to examine transfer beyond AlphaFold-derived data. Together, the benchmark and pretraining method provide a way to assess and improve scalable learning of protein topology.
icml-2026-protein-fold-classification-at.tldr: TEDBench enables large-scale protein fold evaluation, while MiAE learns effective structural representations through heavily masked reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why adapting a language model can damage capabilities it already has. The authors compare supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning across Llama and Qwen models, considering instruction following, general knowledge, and arithmetic reasoning. Their experiments find less forgetting with reinforcement learning, alongside comparable or better performance on the target task.

To explain the difference, they study a simplified model that mixes a prior-knowledge distribution with a target-task distribution. In this setting, reinforcement learning’s mode-seeking behavior can preserve prior knowledge while learning the new task. The authors connect this behavior to on-policy data: training examples generated by the model being updated.

Practical experiments support on-policy data as the source of the observed robustness, rather than other choices such as KL regularization or advantage estimation. The paper also highlights approximately on-policy data as a potentially more efficient option. This suggests a concrete direction for reducing forgetting through data collection, without claiming that reinforcement learning universally eliminates it.
icml-2026-retaining-by-doing-the-role-of.tldr: The study links reinforcement learning’s lower observed forgetting to on-policy data and highlights cheaper approximate alternatives.

paragraphs: Scam2Prompt investigates whether language models reproduce malicious web endpoints in response to ordinary coding requests. The concern is that scam content absorbed during training can later appear in generated code. The paper frames this as a risk that can arise even when the person requesting assistance has a legitimate task.

The auditing pipeline crawls known scam websites, infers their functional purpose, and generates developer-style requests that could expose reproduction of those endpoints. Its benchmark contains 1,377 prompts, all human-validated as benign coding tasks. The audit therefore does not depend on jailbreaks or adversarial instructions to elicit the problematic outputs.

Across seven production models, reported malicious-code generation rates range from 12.9% to 47.3%, with every tested model affected. The authors also find limited protection from leading guardrails and retrieval-augmented agents. These results establish a recurring vulnerability within the benchmark and motivate explicit URL validation in software-development workflows that incorporate model-generated code.
icml-2026-scam2prompt-a-scalable-framewo.tldr: Scam2Prompt finds that benign coding requests can cause production language models to reproduce malicious scam endpoints.

paragraphs: SimpleGPT investigates how Transformer architecture affects the learning rates that training can safely tolerate. The paper connects intermediate activation scales with the Hessian, which describes local curvature of the loss. Its central idea is that controlling activation scale can improve the geometry of optimization and permit larger stable updates.

The authors introduce SimpleNorm, a normalization strategy that stabilizes intermediate activation scales by construction. Their theoretical analysis examines the loss Hessian with respect to network activations and shows a reduction in its spectral norm. This supplies the stated connection between the architectural change and the ability to train with larger learning rates.

Experiments span models with 1, 1.4, 7, and 8 billion parameters. SimpleGPT tolerates learning rates three to ten times larger than standard convention and shows strong optimization stability. In a 7-billion-parameter comparison trained for 60,000 steps, loss falls from 2.290 with Llama2 plus QKNorm to 2.208 with SimpleGPT, providing empirical support for the normalization strategy.
icml-2026-simplegpt-improving-gpt-via-a-.tldr: SimpleNorm stabilizes activation scales, enabling larger stable learning rates and improved reported training performance in GPT models.

paragraphs: SMILE addresses a weakness in prompt optimization: an instruction and a set of examples that work well separately may not work well together. Existing pipelines often optimize these components independently and combine them afterward. The paper instead treats their interaction as part of the selection problem.

The authors observe diminishing returns in in-context-learning performance across diverse instructions. They use this structure to learn an instruction-conditioned surrogate from language-model feedback. Implemented as an Extended Deep Submodular Function, it represents coverage among examples, relevance to the current query, and compatibility with the instruction. A greedy procedure then selects the instruction and demonstrations jointly for each query.

Experiments on six datasets and multiple language-model backbones report consistent improvements over instruction-only, demonstration-only, and existing joint-selection baselines. The findings support optimizing the prompt as an interacting whole. The practical significance is that selection considers which examples suit a particular instruction and question, rather than treating example quality as independent of context.
icml-2026-smile-extended-deep-submodular.tldr: SMILE jointly selects instructions and demonstrations using a learned model of relevance, coverage, and compatibility.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compare several dynamic treatment policies over time. Conventional methods estimate each policy’s counterfactual outcomes separately, preventing information sharing between related policies. The authors show that this separation leaves a second-order bias term structurally uncontrolled and can inflate finite-sample variance even after standard longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood correction.

PEQ-Net addresses the problem by jointly estimating policy-aware versions of the conditional-expectation functions used in longitudinal inference. Its shared policy encoder is trained using kernel mean embeddings so that distances in representation space reflect population-level differences between policies. This creates a structured way to share information while accounting for policy dissimilarity.

After the correction step, the authors prove that the architecture constrains the second-order remainder and stabilizes finite-sample variance. Experiments on semi-synthetic datasets report lower root-mean-square error than existing conditional-expectation methods, especially for closely related policies. The findings connect joint representation learning with more stable comparative causal estimation across multiple policies.
icml-2026-smooth-multi-policy-causal-eff.tldr: PEQ-Net shares representations across treatment policies to stabilize joint causal-effect estimation and reduce reported estimation error.

paragraphs: SPR addresses multimodal classification when some input modalities are missing. Prompt learning can guide a frozen backbone in these situations, but the authors argue that existing approaches underuse the internal structure of prompt vectors. Their method refines that structure to provide more coherent and selective guidance under different missing-input conditions.

The network works at three levels. A global module captures interactions in both directions across prompt layers to reduce inconsistent guidance. A local module organizes neighboring prompt vectors into coherent semantic units. A channel-selection module uses point-wise gating to suppress noise and emphasize useful channels according to which modality is absent.

With only 0.8% trainable parameters, SPR reports significant improvements on three multimodal classification datasets. On MM-IMDB, it exceeds the prior state of the art by a reported 3.8% in F1-Macro at a 90% modality-missing rate. Experiments and ablations support the usefulness of refining prompt structure for robust adaptation while keeping the backbone frozen.
icml-2026-spr-a-structured-prompt-refine.tldr: SPR refines prompt interactions, local structure, and channels to improve multimodal classification when inputs are missing.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether reasoning effort can be measured more meaningfully than by counting generated tokens. Longer chains of thought do not consistently imply greater accuracy and may accompany overthinking. The authors instead examine how predictions change across the model’s internal layers while each token is being produced.

They identify deep-thinking tokens as those whose internal predictions undergo substantial revision in deeper layers before converging. The deep-thinking ratio measures their share of a generated sequence. Across four mathematical and scientific benchmarks and several reasoning-model families, this ratio has a consistently positive correlation with accuracy and outperforms length- and confidence-based measures.

The authors use that signal in Think@n, a strategy that favors candidate generations with higher deep-thinking ratios. Short prefixes allow unpromising generations to be rejected early. Reported results match or exceed standard self-consistency while substantially lowering inference costs. The evidence supports the ratio as a useful selection signal; the reported correlation does not itself establish that increasing the ratio causes better reasoning.
icml-2026-think-deep-not-just-long-measu.tldr: Deep-layer prediction revisions provide a stronger reported accuracy signal than response length and enable cheaper reasoning-sample selection.

paragraphs: This paper examines architectural support for consistent value alignment in language models. The authors argue that value representations are fragile, low-dimensional properties within a rapidly changing residual stream. Steering values directly through that stream therefore faces a mismatch between dynamic internal processing and the stability needed for consistent behavior.

The Stable Value Guidance Transformer introduces an independent value module. It maintains normative representations in a dedicated space separated from the backbone, then translates those signals into learnable latent Bridge Tokens. These tokens guide the generation trajectory, providing an explicit route from the independent value representation to the model’s behavior without disrupting the backbone’s internal representations.

Across multiple backbones and safety benchmarks, SVGT generally reduces harmful scores by more than 70% while preserving generation fluency. These results support independent value modeling as an effective architectural approach in the evaluated settings. The reported reduction is a qualified empirical finding, demonstrating improved guidance rather than establishing universal adherence to human values.
icml-2026-toward-stable-value-alignment-.tldr: SVGT uses an independent value module and Bridge Tokens to reduce harmful outputs while maintaining fluency in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: XSpecMesh addresses the latency of autoregressive mesh generation. These models can produce high-quality meshes with precise topology, but doing so requires thousands or tens of thousands of sequential token predictions. The paper aims to shorten this process while preserving the quality of the generated mesh.

The method adds lightweight decoding heads that propose multiple tokens in parallel during one forward pass. The backbone then verifies each proposed token and resamples those that fail its quality criteria. A distillation strategy trains the lightweight heads to align their prediction distributions with the backbone, increasing the success rate of speculative proposals.

Experiments report a 1.7-fold speedup without a loss of generation quality. The design combines faster proposals with verification by the original model, while distillation makes those proposals more likely to succeed. The result supports speculative decoding as a practical acceleration strategy for long mesh-generation sequences, with the reported quality preservation established through the authors’ experiments.
icml-2026-xspecmesh-quality-preserving-a.tldr: XSpecMesh uses parallel token proposals, backbone verification, and distillation to achieve a reported 1.7-fold mesh-generation speedup without quality loss.
